name: Make-A-Wish America: wishes for children with critical illnesses (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: wishes granted by Make-A-Wish America's national office and 58 chapters to children in the US and its territories.
summary: Make-A-Wish America and its 58 chapters grant wishes (trips, meetings, gifts) to children aged 2½ to 17 with critical illnesses: 16,295 in fiscal 2024 (September 2023 to August 2024), at about $21,600 a wish with fundraising and management. Our model takes the one randomised trial of a wish (quality of life up 0.59 standard deviations against a wait-list, in Israeli children with cancer), lets it fade over about eleven months, adds a share for the family (households of about 3.8) and the hospital costs a wish may save (an observational study found fewer unplanned admissions), which comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000, because a wish costs as much as therapy for dozens of people and buys a few months of better quality of life for one child and some for the family; nothing in the evidence suggests it changes survival. The biggest uncertainties are the size of the effect (one small trial) and how long it lasts (measured once, five weeks after the wish).

rows.label: Cost per wish, with overhead
rows.explainer: Context: about $21,600 a wish with fundraising and management spread over it. Make-A-Wish's own average direct cost of a wish was $10,130 in 2016 (Patel et al. 2019); the rest is staff, chapter running costs and fundraising.

rows.label: Effect on the child's quality of life after the wish (standard deviations)

source.title: Shoshani, Mifano and Czamanski-Cohen (2016), The effects of the Make a Wish intervention on psychiatric symptoms and health-related quality of life of children with cancer: a randomised controlled trial, Quality of Life Research 25(5):1209-1218 (abstract)

rows.explainer: The one randomised trial of a wish: 66 Israeli children aged 5 to 12 with a new diagnosis of life-threatening cancer, randomised to a Make-A-Wish wish (32) or a wait-list (34); the wish was granted 5 to 6 months after baseline and the children measured about 5 weeks after it. Health-related quality of life improved by d = 0.59 against the wait-list (depression 0.70, general distress 0.54, anxiety 0.41, hope 0.71, positive affect 0.80); quality of life is the closest of these to overall wellbeing. No meta-analysis of wishes exists, so there is no prior to blend with; vacation studies (de Bloom 2009: d = 0.43 in adults, faded within weeks) are a different intervention and serve only as a check on size and duration. The 95% interval is ours from the arm sizes (standard error of d about 0.25: 0.10 to 1.08); the abstract gives none.

rows.label: Before the wish: years at the full effect, area-equivalent
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The trial's children chose their wish at baseline and waited 5 to 6 months for it, and the authors credit hope and anticipation; but the trial measured only after the wish, and its wait-list controls were waiting for a wish too, so the measured 0.59 is the wish's effect beyond anticipation and the gain before it is unmeasured. A small rise over the months of waiting: 0.05 years at the full effect (about three weeks), from 0 to 0.25 (the full effect building up over half a year).

rows.label: After the wish: years at the full effect, area-equivalent
rows.explainer: Our judgment, anchored on the one measurement: the full effect was still there 5 weeks after the wish. A holiday's effect on adults fades within weeks of returning to work (de Bloom 2009; a 2023 update with 13 studies finds no difference from before after the first week), but a wish is rarer and larger, and is remembered and retold. About two months at full strength, then a fade over about half a year: 0.17 + 0.5 × 0.5 ≈ 0.4 years at the full effect, from 0.15 (the 5 weeks measured, then a fade over two months) to 1 (a fade over the two years Patel et al. 2019 followed hospital use).

rows.label: Years until the effect has faded (area-equivalent linear fade)
rows.explainer: The two parts above as one linear fade from the full effect with the same area (the triangle's area is half its base): about 0.9 years.

rows.label: Decay of the effect per year (context)
rows.explainer: Context: compare with the decay rates reported in follow-up studies.

rows.label: Continuous discount rate
rows.explainer: The shared yearly rate as a continuous rate, so the effect can be discounted smoothly as it fades.

rows.label: Discount factor over the fading effect
rows.formula: if(continuous_discount_rate > 0, (continuous_discount_rate * effect_duration_years - 1 + exp(-(continuous_discount_rate * effect_duration_years))) / (0.5 * (continuous_discount_rate * effect_duration_years) * (continuous_discount_rate * effect_duration_years)), 1)
rows.explainer: Present value of the triangle (linear fade to zero) at the shared rate, as a share of its undiscounted area; as in the HLI models.

rows.label: SD-years per child
rows.explainer: Area of the triangle: linear decay from the initial effect to zero, discounted.

rows.label: WELLBYs per child
rows.explainer: SD-years into WELLBYs at the site's one rate (@wellby_factors). The WELLBY slider then puts WELLBYs into healthy years.

rows.label: Share of wish children living with two parents
rows.explainer: Our judgment: about seven in ten US children live with two parents (US Census Bureau, America's Families and Living Arrangements, table C3: about 71% in 2023, https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2023/demo/families/cps-2023.html); a serious illness strains some marriages, so 0.7, from 0.6 to 0.8.

rows.label: Household size of a wish child
rows.explainer: Every wish child lives with a family, so the household is a family's with children, not the US average of 2.4 (which counts single people and couples without children): the site's sizes for married couples with school-age children (@household_size.united_states_married_with_children_6_17, 4.2; most wish children are of school age, and all married couples with children average 4.0) and one-parent households (@household_size.united_states_one_parent_with_children, 3.0), from the same survey as the US average, mixed by the share with two parents: about 3.8.

rows.label: Household multiplier
rows.explainer: Each other household member gains the site's one share of the recipient's effect (HLI's, @wellby_factors). Parents and siblings usually share the wish itself (a trip or an experience), so the share may be larger here; no study measures it, and the trial measured only the children.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: Our judgment, the product of two parts. Internal validity 0.65: one small trial (66 children), unblinded, with self- and parent-reported outcomes and many measures reported (the largest, positive affect, not used); small positive trials shrink on replication. External validity 0.75: the trial's children had cancer, were 5 to 12 and lived in Israel; Make-A-Wish America's are 2½ to 17 with many critical illnesses (some too young or too ill to report, anticipate or take in a wish as the trial's children did), and its wishes are similar in kind (trips, meetings, gifts). 0.65 × 0.75 ≈ 0.5, from 0.3 to 0.8. Anchor: the site's psychotherapy models discount single-trial effects by a half or more (HLI's StrongMinds and Friendship Bench analyses shrink a charity's own trial towards the literature by about that much).

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The trial's effect is against a wait-list, so a family's own outings and holidays are already netted out. Below 1 only for a wish the child would have got elsewhere: smaller US wish charities (Dream Factory, Kids Wish Network, Sunshine Foundation) grant a few thousand wishes a year, and Make-A-Wish's chapters have waiting lists (Metro New York and Western New York granted 657 wishes in fiscal 2024 with about 1,000 eligible children waiting at its end, its audited statements, note 14), so few of its children would be served by another. 0.95, from 0.85 to 1.

rows.label: Value of volunteers' time

source.title: Make-A-Wish Foundation of America, audited financial statements, years ended August 31, 2024 and 2023 (CliftonLarsonAllen LLP)
source.page: Note 2, Contributions - Donated Goods and Services, p. 14

rows.explainer: Public-service airtime and space given by media companies, left out of the enterprise's expenses above.

rows.label: Share of the donated media's reported value that is a real resource
rows.explainer: Our judgment: donors value public-service airtime at rates charged for similar advertising, but it fills unsold slots worth far less. Half, from 0.2 to 1 (the reported value).

rows.label: Make-A-Wish's share of the resources behind the wishes
rows.explainer: Convention 2: the network's own spending over everything behind the wishes, including volunteers' time and donated media at its real value; about {{row:attribution_share_shared}}. Donated wish travel and goods (airline miles, hotel stays) are in the enterprise's expenses already. Hospitals' referrals and families' own time aren't counted.

rows.label: Attribution share applied
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Share of counted wishes that work as the trial's did
rows.explainer: 1, so no range: every counted wish is granted. Children too young or too ill to take in a wish as the trial's did are in evidence_adj's external validity, and there is no evidence that smaller wishes do less (Convention 5: no dose discount without a dose-response).

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Measured, so 1: Make-A-Wish's own count of wishes granted meets a randomised trial of the same intervention delivered the same way (a Make-A-Wish wish, chosen by the child and granted by a Make-A-Wish affiliate months later). The trial's narrower population and its size are in evidence_adj.

rows.label: Combined adjustment
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Not modelled, with signs: siblings and grandparents outside the household (+); disappointment where a wish is postponed or the child dies first (−). Lower hospital use has its own rows (deaths section). 2%, from −5% to 10%.

rows.label: Deaths averted per child (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: 0, so no range: no study links a wish to survival; the illnesses are treated as they would be anyway. Lower hospital use is valued below as money saved.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weight for children aged 5 to 14, the middle of wish children's ages, times your value of a life (not used while deaths are 0).

rows.label: Hospital costs saved per wish over the next two years (US$)

source.title: Patel et al. (2019), Impact of a Make-A-Wish experience on healthcare utilization, Pediatric Research 85(5):634-638 (abstract)
source.quote: Wish recipients were 1.9 times more likely to have fewer emergency department visits

rows.explainer: Our judgment from the one study: 496 children granted a wish at Nationwide Children's Hospital (2011-2016) against 496 matched on age, sex, disease and complexity; over two years the wish children were 2.5 times as likely to have fewer unplanned admissions and 1.9 times as likely to have fewer emergency visits, and 2.2 to 2.3 times as likely to have a fall in charges larger than the average wish cost ($10,130). It is observational at one hospital (a wish may be granted when a child's illness has steadied), the savings are in charges, which run well above costs, and the abstract gives no average. $750 of costs per wish over the two years, from 0 (selection explains it all) to $4,000; spread evenly over the two years and discounted (hospital_years).

rows.label: Years over which the hospital savings were observed

source.title: Patel et al. (2019), Impact of a Make-A-Wish experience on healthcare utilization, Pediatric Research 85(5):634-638 (abstract)
source.quote: associated impact on healthcare utilization and costs across 2 years

rows.explainer: The study's follow-up: utilization and costs across 2 years after the wish (Patel et al. 2019). The savings are spread evenly over these years and discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: How the health costs saved are spread, relative to consumption
rows.explainer: Our judgment from the payer mix, on a scale where 1 is a cost proportional to consumption. Children's hospital care is paid by private insurers (premiums per worker, regressive: below 1), Medicaid and CHIP (taxes, near proportional to consumption, but each public dollar saved also saves its cost of raising: above 1) and families' own out-of-pocket costs (close to 1). About 1, from 0.7 to 1.4.

rows.label: Hospital costs saved, in units of value
rows.formula: people_reached * hospital_savings_per_wish / hospital_years * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, hospital_years) * counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * missing_data_adj * $uov_per_ln_consumption / (payer_multiple * @united_states.ce_expenditure_per_person_2024)
rows.explainer: Money saved spread over the many who pay for US health care, each gaining its share of their consumption on the site's log scale (the log curve is straight for small amounts), as the site values US public money: savings over the household survey's consumption per person (@united_states.ce_expenditure_per_person_2024; one scale for US public money, docs/normalization.md 2.14), times the shared value of a doubled income, spread over the years observed and discounted, with the counterfactual, credit, delivery and missing-data adjustments. Not evidence_adj, which is about the quality-of-life trial: the savings judgment carries its own doubt about selection.

rows.label: Deaths averted and hospital costs saved, in units of value
rows.explainer: Deaths averted (none) and the hospital costs saved, both in units of value, so they reach WELLBYs only through the bridge below.

rows.label: Deaths averted and hospital costs saved, in WELLBYs
rows.explainer: The one row that puts units of value into WELLBYs; the WELLBY unit's conversion multiplies it back, so deaths and money count exactly their shared value at any WELLBY rate.

rows.label: WELLBYs from the year's wishes
rows.formula: people_reached * wellbys_per_person * household_multiplier * total_adj * (1 + unmodelled_benefits_adj) + wellbys_from_uov
rows.explainer: Children's and families' WELLBYs times the adjustments, plus the unmodelled benefits and harms.
